chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Dedicated to Lanie Chipkin and Chloe Murray,
the Wolf and the Bee.
Major support for this volume was provided by Naval Ravikant.
Additional support by Daniel Gilbert, Diego Rey, Mike Maples, Jr., Allos AI, and Ben Ferrum.
Conjecture Institute gratefully acknowledges their generosity in advancing this work.

If we really do live in a quantum multiverse, then where does gravity fit into that picture? How does quantum theory solve the problem of time? How can the world be truly local, despite quantum theory’s notoriously bizarre properties? Can we ever settle the debate over whether entropy is subjective or objective? What is the relationship between probability and fundamental reality?

_Bold Conjectures, Volume II: Essays Across Physics_ consists of essays by physicists who explore and answer questions such as these. Drawing from their own careers as researchers, contributors to this entry in our Bold Conjectures series either explain cutting-edge developments in physics that most people are not yet aware of, or they clarify a key idea that popular culture tends to get wrong.

In this compendium, you’ll also read about novel ways by which we may test for quantum effects in biology, the history of string theory, the philosophy of effective realism, a new way to test the nature of gravity, and what constructor theory of information may tell us about how to bring together general relativity and quantum theory.

Each essay may be read independently of the others, though often you will discover that ideas in one essay reinforce those in another. Like the human project that is science itself, _Bold Conjectures, Volume II: Essays Across Physics_ has no singular starting point or end point but rather consists of a collection of explanations, advancements, and open problems that the reader is encouraged to explore as he or she sees fit.

Thanks to all of the physicists who kindly contributed to this compendium: Abdullah Afzal, Julian Barbour, Charles Alexandre Bédard, Giuseppe Di Pietra, Aditya Iyer, Sam Kuypers, Chiara Marletto, Simone Rijavec, Hassaan Saleem, Mia Stamatova, Vlatko Vedral, Maria Violaris, David Wallace, and Antonia Weber.

I thank David Kedmey for his indispensable role in producing the second entry in our Bold Conjectures series, and I thank Aaron Stupple for his countless suggestions during the course of this book’s creation.
Yours,
Logan Chipkin
President & Cofounder, Conjecture Institute

chapters.title: 1 — The Fate of Spacetime
paragraphs: What Many Worlds Means for Gravity
Sam Kuypers

Modern physics consists of two pillars, namely general relativity, which explains spacetime and the mutual interaction between matter and it; and quantum theory, which explains practically everything else. Each of them separately is superbly explanatory and provides a thorough and unintuitive overhaul of our best theories that came before.

These two pillars do not merely describe distinct, non-overlapping domains. Physical reality is a single, unified whole, and it is therefore unsurprising that the two theories overlap. Yet despite this overlap, they resist unification into a single, comprehensive framework. The task of unifying them has been a long-standing problem, one that has baffled physicists for almost a century. But what, exactly, stands in the way? Why do these two theories fail to work together naturally?
To understand this, we must first study both theories and see what they tell us about the world.
General Relativity

General relativity divides physical reality into two kinds of systems. First, there is spacetime, which is the arena in which motion occurs. Second, there is matter and energy, which exist and move within spacetime. In relativity, due to the famous E = mc², matter and energy are not distinct; instead they are a single physical quantity, so matter and energy can be treated as interchangeable.[1]

In pre-Einsteinian theories of space and time, such as Isaac Newton’s theory of gravity, space, time, matter, and energy were treated as distinct entities. The presence of matter and energy could not influence space or time, since the former acted instead as a static background against which motion occurred. Nor were space and time understood as parts of a larger structure with well-defined physical properties. All of these assumptions are overturned by general relativity. Space and time are unified into a single entity called spacetime, which is a physical system in its own right, one with unexpected properties. For instance, the presence of matter and energy affects spacetime by curving it: spacetime can buckle and bend, taking on shapes that are unfamiliar in Newtonian gravity. In turn, the shape of spacetime influences the motion of matter within it, which is how general relativity accounts for gravity.

All of these counterintuitive consequences result from simple, elegant principles that Einstein adopted, such as locality: the idea that doing something to a system cannot influence a remote one. This principle is violated by Newtonian gravity, since in that theory the force of gravity acts instantaneously, affecting all masses in the universe immediately (though increasingly weakly the further away the mass is). In general relativity, this is not the case, as any disturbance in a region of spacetime requires a finite time to propagate to another region. Hence, according to general relativity, were the Sun to suddenly disappear by some magic, we on Earth would not notice this until roughly eight minutes later.

Einstein built general relativity as a means to satisfy this and other principles. Thus, although the theory is counterintuitive and highly detailed, it follows from elegant, simple, and sensible assumptions. The plethora of predictions it makes—from the existence of black holes, to the bending of star light during a solar eclipse, to the anomalous precession of Mercury’s perihelion—are but some of the empirical tests that general relativity has been subjected to and withstood.

Importantly, general relativity is a high-level theory about two kinds of systems: spacetime and the matter and energy inside it. It is up to low-level (subsidiary) theories to specify details such as the initial distribution of matter and energy or the particular forms they take. One might assume, for instance, the presence of electromagnetic fields, or simply a spherical mass, or a thin mist of matter such as exists in a nebula, among many other possibilities. All of these can be incorporated into the framework of general relativity, which then determines how spacetime and its contents evolve through their mutual interaction.
Quantum Theory

Like general relativity, quantum theory is not a theory of specific systems. Rather, it is a set of principles used to construct theories that describe a retinue of physical systems. There is a quantum theory of the atom, which is distinct from the quantum theory of the electromagnetic field, which is again distinct from the quantum theories of the weak and strong nuclear forces, and so forth. There are many more such theories, often radically different from one another, except in that they obey the principles of quantum theory. Here we will discuss the three most important principles.

The first is that, when a quantum system can be in either state A or in state B, it can also be in a state that is a superposition of A and B, meaning that the system is in both states simultaneously. For example, if it is possible for a system to be in one location or in another, then it should be possible for the system to be in both locations at once; some systems have spin, a property somewhat analogous to a magnetic moment, which can be “up” or “down”, and hence such particles can have both spins at once; if a qubit can be in state “0” and in state “1”, then it can be in both states at the same time; and so forth. This is aptly called the superposition principle.

Remarkably, whenever a system is in a superposition of states A and B, it is never observed as being in a state that does both things simultaneously. Instead, an observation will cause it to collapse into either A or B, meaning that, with a certain probability provided by quantum theory, one will observe the system either in state A or in state B. This is illustrated by Schrödinger’s famous thought experiment, aptly called Schrödinger’s cat. A cat is placed in a box together with a radioactive particle and a vial of poison that is released if the particle decays. According to quantum theory, before observing the contents of the box, the particle is in a superposition of having decayed and not having decayed, and so the cat is in a superposition of being alive and dead. Yet when the box is opened, the cat is always found either alive or dead; we would never find these two versions of the cat in the box at once. The same is true of all other superposition states.

As such, our evidence for a system having been in a superposition is always indirect. How, then, do we know that it can be in a superposition? The answer is that the different components of the superposition can be made to _interfere_ with one another, i.e., the two _instances_ of the system—the one in state A and the one in state B—can affect each other so as to produce outcomes that would be physically impossible if the system had not been in a superposition. Such experimental demonstrations are called _interference experiments_.

A classic example is the double-slit experiment. A particle of light, called a photon, is sent towards a barrier with two slits and passes through both. Immediately upon passing through the barrier, the photon is therefore in a superposition of instances: one instance of the photon passed through the left slit, and the other instance passed through the right one. This is not a case of the photon having turned into two photons. There is only ever one—if observed, one would find it only in one location. Nonetheless, this single photon can do multiple things at once, like go through both slits. Having passed through the two slits, the photon then strikes a screen at a particular spot. After repeating the experiment with many photons (each sent through individually, in sequence) a pattern arises of bright and dark fringes, called an interference pattern. That pattern is due to the two instances of each photon having interacted with each other.

It is notable that when one of the two slits is closed, the interference pattern disappears. With only a single slit open, the pattern on the screen reduces to a diffuse spot that gradually tapers off, as there are no different instances of the photon to interact with one another. When both slits are open, the photon does pass through both slits so that there are two instances. These then interact by recombining at certain locations on the screen, reinforcing one another and making detection at those locations more likely. At other locations, they interact by cancelling, so that no photon is ever detected there. These processes of merging and cancelling are known respectively as constructive interference and destructive interference.

A striking implication is that, when both slits are open, photons detected at the bright fringes cannot simply have passed through only one of the slits. A photon reaches such locations only because it branched into two instances, each passing through one of the slits, and later recombining at the bright fringes. Likewise, the dark fringes are locations where the two instances cancel each other out. Physically, the instances contributing at the bright fringes therefore really did pass through both slits. Nothing in the experimental setup, neither detectors nor environmental records, can indicate which slit the photon passed through, because there is no fact about which path it took except that it went through both.

This feature is not unique to the interference pattern observed in the double-slit experiment. All interference experiments demonstrate that a system was in a superposition because the observed state could only have been reached if the system previously occupied multiple alternative states at once that later interfered with one another.
Entanglement

A second, crucial property of quantum systems—perhaps the property that most clearly distinguishes them from classical systems—is _entanglement_. This can be explained as follows. Consider a particle that is in a superposition of being half at location x and half at location y, with sufficient separation such that an interaction at x cannot influence anything at y (see Figure 2).[2] Now suppose there is a second, incoming particle, which initially has a definite location and travels towards location x. Since the delocalised particle is in a superposition of being at x and at y, what happens when the incoming particle reaches x? Does it interact as if the delocalised particle were only half-present, and therefore get half-deflected? How does Nature turn this into a coherent physical story?

According to quantum theory, the resolution is as follows. When the incoming particle reaches x, it itself enters a superposition of two states. One of these states is such that the incoming particle encounters the delocalised one at x, interacts with it, and is deflected exactly as it would be if the delocalised particle were fully present at that position. The other state is such that the incoming particle finds that the delocalised one is not at x (being at position y instead), and hence it does not interact with the particle, continuing along its original trajectory instead (see Figure 3). Both of these histories occur simultaneously, so the incoming particle is in a superposition of having been deflected and not having been deflected.

Moreover, this is a superposition of a special kind, as the state of the delocalised particle are correlated with the state of the incoming particle. The joint system is in a superposition of the states “the delocalised particle is at x and collided with the incoming particle” and “the delocalised particle is at y and the incoming particle continues undisturbed”. When a composite system is in such a state, it is said to be entangled.

Because quantum systems can be in superpositions, any system that can interact with another must also be capable of becoming entangled with it. Entanglement is therefore not an optional feature of quantum theory; it is required for consistency.
Universality of Quantum Theory

The final, most controversial principle determines the way in which quantum systems evolve. Generally, such systems will obey what is called unitary evolution, which is continuous (i.e., a system smoothly changes from one state to another), deterministic (i.e., given an initial state, it produces a definite final state) and reversible (i.e., if the laws of physics allow a system to evolve from state A to state B, they also allow it to evolve from B to A). This is the type of evolution that is, for example, described by Schrödinger’s famous equation, and describes processes such as interference.

However, this type of evolution conflicts with the aforementioned phenomenon of collapse, which occurs during a “measurement”. Collapse is discontinuous, probabilistic, and non-reversible, making the two types of evolution (unitary and collapse) hard to reconcile with one other. Notably, I have not defined what a measurement is, as there is no consensus on what counts as a measurement in regard to the collapse postulate. There are intuitive ideas, such as: “A measurement occurs when a scientist in a lab uses lab equipment to determine the position of a particle.” That is not a theory of measurement but rather just an intuitive description. A theory should describe what it is about the scientists and the lab equipment that can produce collapse.

Many potential solutions have been put forward over the years, most of which fail to solve the problem or, worse, contaminate otherwise successful explanations. For example, Wigner thought that it was the scientist’s consciousness that was the determining factor in producing collapse. But even if that were true (it is not), it is not an explanation of why a conscious entity like a scientist can produce collapse. There is not even an explanation of what consciousness is, so if anything, this attempt at solving the problem only amplifies our confusion. Others have posited that collapse happens because large things (e.g., people and lab equipment, which are large relative to atoms) behave differently from the small stuff that quantum theory describes. Large systems are supposed to be described by classical physics, whereas small things are described by quantum theory.

This second line of inquiry is undoubtedly more physical than the idea that consciousness has a role to play in fundamental physics. It is physical enough that it, in principle, allows for experimental tests. For instance, the theory that large systems are described by classical physics would be refuted if large systems were shown to have quantum properties, such as being able to be in a superposition.

Interference experiments are typically hard to perform on large systems. But the size of systems on which such experiments can be performed has been increasing. For example, Anton Zeilinger and others[3] have performed interference experiments on fullerene molecules, often called buckyballs, pushing the limits of what was previously thought possible. In a similar vein, John Clarke, Michel Devoret, and John Martinis have recently been awarded the 2025 Nobel Prize for demonstrating that macroscopic systems also exhibit quantum properties.[4] These discoveries undermine the view that large systems must be described by classical physics rather than quantum theory.

This raises the question: which systems, if any, are not described by quantum theory? This line of thought led Hugh Everett III[5] to conclude that there is no such limit. Quantum theory is universal: everything made of fundamental particles, such as electrons, neutrons, photons, and so forth, must be described quantum mechanically. As such, Everett posited that measuring instruments, which are themselves made of atoms, must also be described by quantum theory and so must adhere to the same principles hitherto discussed, such as the superposition principle, the possibility of entanglement, and unitary evolution.

If Everett’s scheme is to work, he must somehow get rid of collapse, as it is the reason to suppose there might be a cut-off to quantum theory’s universality. So, how does one unify these two different types of evolution, given their distinct and even opposing properties? Everett proposed that entanglement can explain the appearance of collapse.

In Everett’s model of measurement, a measuring instrument (or measurer) interacts with a system so that its final state reflects the state of the system being measured. This is already familiar from classical physics. A mercury thermometer, for example, correlates the temperature of its environment with the height of its mercury column so that, when the temperature rises, the mercury expands, and when it falls, the mercury contracts.

The same pattern appears in quantum theory. If the system being measured has one definite state, call it X, the measurer records that state such that it outputs “the system was in state X”. Everett realised that if the quantum system being measured is in a superposition of several states at once, the measurer responds to all of them by becoming entangled with the system. Rather than selecting a single outcome, the interaction between the measurer and the system gives rise to multiple outcomes, each reflected in a different instance of the measurer. Hence, quantum theory describes the state after the measurement as a collection of universes or branches,[6] each defined by a distinct measurement outcome. Everett’s solution works because in each branch, it appears as if at random only a single, definite outcome was recorded and that the other outcomes have simply disappeared, just as if collapse had happened. Thus, quantum theory describes a multiverse in which all the different possible outcomes of a measurement appear in some universe, which is why Everett’s solution is often called the many-worlds interpretation.

These same features were already apparent in the earlier example of the delocalised particle and the incoming particle. After their interaction, the multiverse contains different branches. In one branch, the incoming particle collided with the delocalised one because that particle was at position x. In another branch, the incoming particle is not deflected, since the delocalised particle was at position y. Already in this simple example, we can see why collapse appears to occur. In the branch in which the incoming particle is deflected, it encounters the delocalised particle as if it were fully present at position x. The alternative possibility, in which the particle was at position y, seems to have disappeared. But it has not: it is simply in another branch.

Thus, each branch contains a single, definite outcome of a measurement, which appears to be selected at random (with a certain probability) from the various alternative outcomes. This is why observers experience a world in which something definite has happened, making it seems as if there were collapse. From the perspective of multiverse as a whole, however, evolution is deterministic, since it is certain that all possible alternative outcomes are realised in some branch. What appears to be the result of an irreversible and probabilistic collapse process within a single branch is in fact the consequence of deterministic and reversible unitary evolution.
Decoherence

Why is it so hard to detect that there are other universes? One reason is that other universes are hidden from view after a measurement, as we can only see our own universe, not the ones that are inhabited by our counterparts. When we open the box containing Schrödinger’s cat, for instance, only a single version of the cat is observed, with the other version belonging to a different branch of the multiverse. But this is only part of the explanation, since it does not by itself rule out the possibility of interference between branches.

After all, even for small systems, the principal way to demonstrate that they were in a superposition is through interference experiments. Such experiments are difficult to perform with large systems because interference merges two possible alternatives into a single outcome, which requires that there are no records left of the alternative states the system was in. Many-worlds offers a natural explanation of why that is. If two different universes are to recombine into a single one, as happens during interference, then the properties that initially differentiated those universes must become identical. That includes any records that contain information about which state a system was in before an interference experiment. Hence, for two universes to merge via interference, either such records should be erased beforehand, or they should be reset via the interference process itself.

Large systems, like people, are constantly interacting with their environment, leaving traces of their position, momentum, magnetisation, volume, and so on. For large systems to interfere, it is therefore not enough for the systems themselves to recombine; all parts of the environment that carry information about the systems’ state would also have to interfere with their counterparts. Any information that distinguishes the alternatives must be eliminated, since such information cannot remain after the interference experiment.

A football rolling across a field illustrates the problem. As it moves, it leaves traces of its path in the grass, the air, and the surrounding radiation. For the football to interfere with its counterparts in other branches, not only the football but also the entire field and everything else that recorded its motion would need to interfere as well, or that information would somehow have to be removed. But this quickly becomes a runaway process since the field itself continues to leave traces of _its_ own state in ever larger parts of _its_ environment. This is why interference between branches is not merely unlikely for macroscopic objects, but practically impossible.

This process in which a quantum system interacts significantly with its environment and thereby leaves records is known as _decoherence_, and as explained above, it suppresses interference between different instances of a quantum system. As a result, although large systems are quantum systems, they generally exhibit little to no interference effects. Hence, some of their properties can be described by classical physics to a very good approximation. This is never true of all of a system’s properties, but it is often true of those relevant for everyday motion, such as the centre of mass of the aforementioned football.
A Fundamental Tension

With the principles of quantum theory in place, we can return to the problem of unifying quantum theory and general relativity. As discussed, almost everything in Nature is described by quantum theory: all matter and energy are quantum, since all matter consists of fundamental particles such as photons, electrons, and gluons. This is intriguing because general relativity is about two separate systems: spacetime and the matter and energy inside it, and it treats both systems as being classical. That is to say, according to general relativity, there can be no such thing as a superposition of particles. From this perspective, the natural question is not why general relativity and quantum theory resist unification, but why is it that, if quantum theory is true, general relativity works as a description at all?

It is often said that general relativity and quantum theory can be treated separately because the former applies to very large systems, such as planets and stars, while the latter applies only to very small ones. However, as established in the previous sections, this is false. Quantum theory is our best explanation of atoms, and large systems such as planets and stars are composed of atoms, a fact that is often crucial. Neutron stars, for instance, are supported against gravitational collapse by quantum effects.[7]

The real reason quantum theory and gravity can be made to “play nicely” together at all, at least approximately, is that large systems are highly decohered and follow roughly classical trajectories. The different branches corresponding to different trajectories practically do not interfere with one another. Consider the Earth, for instance. It is a quantum system consisting of many atoms (roughly 10⁵⁰ of them), which are constantly interacting with their environment, leaving traces of themselves, and therefore thoroughly decohering. Since it is a quantum system, we know that the Earth is a multiversal object and that there must exist many instances of it in other branches of the multiverse, each defined by a slightly different, approximately classical trajectory. The other branches are effectively autonomous from each other due to the effects of decoherence, so little to no interference occurs between them. As a result, we can treat the Earth as classical and pretend that it has a single, definite centre of mass and trajectory, even though this is strictly speaking false. Under this assumption, general relativity can be used to determine how the Earth curves spacetime, how it moves around the Sun, and so on.

While we can pretend that the Earth has a single, classical trajectory, in reality the Earth is constantly branching into distinct instances that follow slightly different trajectories. The same is true of the Moon, and the Sun, all the other planets in the Solar System, and beyond. In each branch, spacetime must therefore be curved differently, since the mass distribution differs in each of them. So, for example, in a universe in which the Sun has a different location than it does in ours, spacetime must have a different shape. General relativity, however, allows only a spacetime with a definite curvature. It does not permit superpositions of different spacetime curvatures to exist. The fundamental tension is that masses can be in superpositions, but spacetime (which interacts with masses inside it by curving) cannot be in a superposition. This is what prevents unification. To solve it, a quantum description of spacetime is needed.
The Path Towards Unification

Physicists have tried for nearly a century to unify general relativity and quantum theory without success. Some luminaries have even suggested that perhaps the attempt at unifying the two theories is misguided and unnecessary. For example, Dyson[8] has suggested that a theory of quantum gravity would make solely untestable predictions and would therefore be scientifically uninteresting:

If this hypothesis were true, it would imply that theories of quantum gravity are untestable and scientifically meaningless. The classical universe and the quantum universe could then live together in peaceful coexistence. No incompatibility between the two pictures could ever be demonstrated.

In short, Dyson’s argument is that issues which are philosophically irksome need not trouble scientists. But even if, for the sake of argument, we assume that Dyson is right and that in principle a theory of quantum gravity could not make predictions, which seems unlikely, the philosophical issues associated with such a theory cannot simply be erased from physics. The superposition principle is central to quantum theory, yet it is unclear how it can be reconciled with general relativity. If a mass can be in two locations at once, and spacetime is curved by the matter within it, then how could spacetime respond to such a matter distribution if it is not itself allowed to be in superposition? There is no known way.

Attempts to treat spacetime as a quantum system have been made. A notable example is the theory of Wheeler & DeWitt, the central result of which is the Wheeler–DeWitt equation. One of its implications is that the multiverse must be completely frozen, as the equation requires the multiverse to be stationary and unchanging, a result that was initially mystifying. A beautiful solution was to respond that this is to be expected: spacetime itself shouldn’t evolve, as time and dynamical evolution exist inside spacetime. As such, when you have a description of the whole of physical reality, including spacetime, that entire description must be fundamentally stationary. This insight was later generalised by Page & Wootters, who showed that one can dispense with the external time parameter that is usually assumed to exist in quantum theory, and that time can instead be treated as something that emerges from the (stationary) quantum state. In their account, as in the theory of Wheeler & DeWitt, the whole of physical reality is timeless, but time can be recovered as something within different branches of the multiverse. As Deutsch[9] has put it, different times turn out to be different universes.

The Wheeler–DeWitt equation remains enigmatic, but the Page–Wootters construction that it inspired has drastically increased our understanding of the nature of time, of which we now have a robust quantum theory in the non-relativistic case. What remains problematic is how to treat space in a similar way so that it emerges from more elementary properties of quantum systems, as is the case for time.

These insights sit particularly naturally with the many-worlds interpretation. If time can already be incorporated into quantum theory as something internal to the multiverse, then there is no principled obstacle to doing the same for space. With the benefit of hindsight, this way of treating time is reminiscent of Everett’s treatment of measurement. In both cases, there appears to be a classical structure mixed in with our quantum theory—in the case of measurement, we assumed that there was a classical world in which outcomes had definite values, whereas in the case of time, we had to assume that there is an external time parameter relative to which system can change. In both cases, the solution is to treat that classical structure as superfluous, to remove it, and to replace it with a quantum model instead, as summarised in the table below.
Time Measurement
The unnecessary structure is external, classical time external, macroscopic classical world
Seems necessary to explain dynamics explain why we see only one definite outcome
It can be removed since different moments of time are realised in different universes different measurement outcomes are realised in different universes

Now that time is understood as emerging naturally from quantum theory, such that it does not have to appear as a classical parameter put in by hand, it becomes difficult to treat space any differently. Likewise, it is equally difficult to maintain interpretations of quantum theory that rely on external classical structures, as all non-Everettian interpretations do. On this view, the many-worlds interpretation is not an optional philosophical gloss but a natural completion of the quantum description of the reality. We are still left with the quest of unifying quantum theory and gravity, which has hitherto eluded us. But these recent advances point to a clear path forward for how to give a quantum description of not just time but potentially also space and ultimately spacetime. Hence, it might be that what is needed to understand quantum gravity is not just new ideas, but also the courage to take our existing principles seriously.
[1] In fact, E = mc² is not the full equation, as it only describes massive particles at rest. The full equation is _E_² = _p_²_c_² + _m_²_c_⁴, where p is a particle’s momentum.

[2] In the figures we treat the particles as having well-defined positions and trajectories. More precisely, the particles should be understood as sufficiently massive systems prepared in narrow centre-of-mass wavepackets (or, for one of the particles, a superposition of two such wavepackets), so that in each branch of the state the positions and momenta are well defined to a good approximation and wavepacket spreading during the interaction is negligible.
[3] Arndt M, Nairz O, Vos-Andreae J, Keller C, van der Zouw G, Zeilinger A. Wave–particle duality of C₆₀ molecules. _Nature_. 1999;401:680–682.
[4] Nobel Prize in Physics 2025. NobelPrize.org. Available from: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/summary/ (accessed 22 January 2026).

[5] Everett H III. The theory of the universal wave function. In: DeWitt BS, Graham N, editors. _The Many-Worlds Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics_. Princeton (NJ): Princeton University Press; 1973. p. 3–140.
[6] The terms “universes” and “branches” will be used interchangeably.
[7] The Pauli exclusion principle prevents fermions from occupying the same energy states, generating an outward pressure that counteracts gravity.

[8] How incompatible worldviews can coexist. Ideas | Institute for Advanced Study (Institute Letter Spring 2013). Available from: https://www.ias.edu/ideas/2013/dyson-graviton (accessed 22 January 2026).
[9] Deutsch D. _The Fabric of Reality_. London: Penguin Books; 1997.
