chapters.title: 5 — Sherlock Photon
paragraphs: A Quantum Witness to Non-Classicality in Biology
Giuseppe Di Pietra

At the end of the nineteenth century, physics was widely believed to be a _completed science_, with no further surprises left in store. Many prominent scientists thought that the fundamental laws governing Nature had already been discovered, and that future progress would consist mainly in refining measurements rather than uncovering new principles. No further conceptual revolutions were anticipated. This sentiment was famously expressed by Albert A. Michelson in a speech at the University of Chicago in 1894.[1] Michelson—the same physicist behind the Michelson–Morley experiment that ruled out the existence of the luminiferous ether, the hypothetical medium through which light was thought to propagate[2]—remarked:

“[I]t seems probable that most of the grand underlying principles have been firmly established and that further advances are to be sought chiefly in the rigorous application of these principles to all the phenomena which come under our notice. It is here that the science of measurement shows its importance—where quantitative work is more to be desired than qualitative work. An eminent physicist remarked that the future truths of physical science are to be looked for in the sixth place of decimals.”

The “grand principles” Michelson referred to were those of what we now call classical physics, encompassing classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics. With hindsight, however, we know how dramatically mistaken this view was.

Only six years later, the German physicist Max Planck discovered that classical physics was unable to explain the observed spectrum of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a perfect absorber, known as a _black body_. To resolve this discrepancy between theory and experiment, Planck proposed a radical idea: electromagnetic energy could be exchanged only in _discrete packets_, or _quanta_, with energy E_(quantum) = hν, where h is Planck’s constant and ν the frequency of the radiation. Planck himself regarded this assumption as a mathematical expedient.[3] Yet five years later, Albert Einstein took this idea a step further, conjecturing that the energy “quanta” were not just a calculation trick but corresponded to _real_ physical entities: the particles that mediate electromagnetic interactions, now known as _photons_.[4] The necessity of such an assumption to resolve the so-called _ultraviolet catastrophe_, and thus to explain the blackbody spectrum, came as a profound shock. It marked the first major failure of classical physics and revealed one of the two “clouds”—as Lord Kelvin famously called the unresolved anomalies threatening the foundations of classical physics—in his 1900 lecture at the Royal Institution in London.[5] This was the dawn of one of the most successful and unsettling theories in the history of science: _quantum theory_, also known as _quantum mechanics_.[6]

The emergence of quantum theory was not merely the introduction of a new physical constant or a correction to existing laws. It represented a much deeper rupture, a change in the very way physical reality is described and understood. To appreciate how radically quantum mechanics departs from classical intuition, let us begin with a familiar example.

Imagine tossing a fair coin. The outcomes heads (H) and tails (T) each occur with probability 1/2, i.e., if we toss the coin multiple times without recording each result, we will get H half of the time on average. If we toss the coin twice and record the outcomes, the four possible sequences (HH, TT, HT, and TH) each occur with probability 1/4, since the two events are independent and the joint probability is the product of the individual ones.[7] There is nothing mysterious here. The probabilistic description merely reflects our ignorance of the detailed dynamics of the coin. In principle, if we knew the force, angle, spin, and air resistance with sufficient precision (the _initial conditions_ of the classical system), classical mechanics would allow us to predict the outcome of each individual toss with certainty. The randomness lies not in the coin itself, but in our lack of information.

Let us now attempt to apply the same reasoning to a quantum system, for example a photon. Consider the scheme in Fig. 1, a Mach–Zehnder interferometer. This optical device splits a photon into two possible paths using the reflective and transmissive properties of a first beam splitter, reflects the paths with mirrors, and recombines them at a second beam splitter before detection. If the photon behaved like a classical coin, it would choose one path or the other with probability 1/2, and after recombination it would emerge from either output port with equal probability. Each of the four possible histories—00, 01, 10, 11—would then occur with probability 1/4.
This expectation is entirely reasonable. It is also entirely wrong.

When no additional disturbances are present in the two interferometer’s arms, the photon always triggers the same detector D0, with probability 1 . The probabilities do not combine as they would for a classical random process. Something fundamentally different is at work.
What Makes Quantum Physics Different?
To understand what is different in the Mach–Zehnder interferometer, it is useful to recall what classical physics assumes about the world.

In classical mechanics,[8] physical systems are described in terms of quantities such as position and velocity. At any given instant, an object is assumed to occupy a precise point in space and to move with a well-defined speed and direction. These quantities are not only conceptually well-defined but also, at least in principle, _simultaneously measurable with arbitrary precision_.[9] This assumption is so deeply ingrained in our everyday experience that it rarely attracts attention. A football, a car, or a planet is always _somewhere_, moving in _some way_. Even when it has multiple options to choose from, this system is _always_ in a _single one_ of them. Given sufficient information about the initial conditions of a system and the forces acting upon it, classical mechanics allows us to predict its future evolution exactly. The motion of the system unfolds along a well-defined _trajectory_, a continuous sequence of positions ordered in time. This deterministic picture is encapsulated in Isaac Newton’s _second law of motion_,[10]

which states that a force F⃗ acting on a body of mass m determines its acceleration a⃗.[11] Once the forces and initial conditions are specified, the future of the system is, in principle, fully determined. For more than two centuries, this framework proved extraordinarily successful. There was little reason to doubt its universal validity.

It would thus be tempting to explain the behaviour of the photon going through the Mach–Zehnder interferometer in the very same way. We might assume that the photon must have taken one path _or_ the other and attempt to assign it a precise position at a given time, measure its velocity, and reconstruct its trajectory using Eq. 1. However, experiments soon revealed that this programme cannot be carried out.

The more precisely one determines the position of the photon, the less precisely its velocity can be known, and vice versa. This is not due to imperfect instruments, nor to experimental clumsiness. It is a _fundamental feature_ of Nature itself. This is the essence of the _uncertainty principle_, introduced by Werner Heisenberg in 1927,[12] two years after the publication of the work that conventionally marks the birth of quantum mechanics.[13] Although commonly associated with position and velocity (or, more precisely, position and momentum), the principle has a much broader scope. It applies to entire classes of physical quantities—the system’s _observables_—that cannot be simultaneously specified with arbitrary precision. Observables that cannot be simultaneously measured to arbitrary precision are called _incompatible_.[14] Measuring one of them with increasing precision inevitably reduces the precision with which the other can be known. The crucial point is this: at the microscopic scale, the very notion of a well-defined trajectory breaks down. Quantum systems do not move along paths in the classical sense. Asking for “the position and velocity of a photon at the same time” is not merely difficult; it is conceptually ill-posed.
We may therefore define a _quantum_, or _non-classical_, system as follows:[15]
Definition 1. _A physical system is non-classical when it must be described by a minimum of two incompatible observables._
Superposition and Interference: The Role of Quantum Coherence
We are now in a position to understand the behaviour of the photon in the interferometer.

If two observables are incompatible, there exists no state of the system in which both have definite values. With respect to the observable that is not measured, the system may exist in multiple states _simultaneously_, with different probabilities of observing it in one or the other determined by the physical dynamics. The probability of observing the system in a certain state of the superposition determines its weight. In each of these states, this observable takes a different value, revealed only upon measurement. This phenomenon is known as _quantum superposition_ and represents one of the most distinctive features of the quantum world.

Returning to the Mach–Zehnder interferometer shown in Fig. 1, the effect of the beam splitter is to create a superposition of the photon’s position in two distinct branches of the interferometer: branch 0, described by state |0⟩, and branch 1, described by state |1⟩. For a symmetric beam splitter, i.e., one capable of reflecting and transmitting light equally, the two branches have equal weight; for an asymmetric one, the weights differ, while remaining fully admissible within quantum mechanics. We may therefore write the state of the photon after the first beam splitter as |ψ⟩ = a₀|0⟩ + a₁|1⟩, where a₀ and a₁ are the coefficients of the superposition, determining the weight of each branch, also known as the _relative_ phase between the branches. The second beam splitter plays a role analogous to the first. However, since the incoming photon is now in the state |ψ⟩, a superposition of two different positions, the recombination of the two branches allows them to interfere. In this particular case, this interference _closes_ the superposition and returns the photon to a definite output port, |0⟩, which explains why only detector D0 clicks. A classical model would predict that, given many experimental runs, one or the other detector would click with equal frequency.

The phenomenon of quantum superposition becomes even more striking in another experiment that has puzzled physicists since the earliest days of quantum theory: the double-slit experiment, schematised in Fig. 2. Consider a source of monochromatic radiation, idealised so as to emit one photon at a time. In front of the source is an opaque screen containing two narrow slits, which can be opened or closed at will. Behind the screen, a second photographic plate records the arrival of the photons as small luminous spots.

We now send one photon at a time towards the screen with both slits open (Fig. 2(a)) and deliberately refrain from observing what happens during their journey. We simply wait for a pattern to emerge on the photographic plate. If photons behaved like classical particles, each would pass through one slit or the other, and the detection screen would gradually display two bright bands corresponding to the slit positions. Each photon would contribute a single spot aligned with either the left or the right opening.

This is not what is observed. Instead, a full interference pattern appears on the detection screen! Bright and dark fringes emerge that are characteristic of constructive and destructive interference, exactly as one would expect from _waves_. It is as if, despite sending one photon at a time, two waves had been generated at the slits and had interfered with each other—much like the ripples formed on the surface of a pond when two stones are thrown into it. And yet, there was only a single photon.

The unavoidable conclusion is that the photon did not pass through one slit or the other, as a classical particle would. Rather, it passed through _both_ slits simultaneously. The photon existed in a superposition of two states—passing through the left slit and the right slit—just as it occupied both arms of the interferometer at the same time after the first beam splitter. Because the photon was present at both slits, each slit effectively acted as a source of radiation, allowing interference to occur. This phenomenon is known as _quantum interference_, which arises from the relative phase between the branches of a single quantum system’s superposition. The ability of a quantum system to maintain this relative phase is called _quantum coherence_. It is coherence that allows a linear combination of physical states to be itself a valid physical state—clearest manifestations of the principle of superposition—in much the same way as overlapping waves can produce observable interference patterns.

If one of the two slits is now closed (Fig. 2(b)), for example the left one, the interference pattern disappears. Only a single band remains on the screen, aligned with the open slit. The photon is now forced to pass through that single slit; it can no longer exist in a superposition of two paths, because one of the possible alternatives has been removed.
There is, however, an even subtler effect.

If both slits are left open but we attempt to monitor which slit the photon passes through on its way to the screen (Fig. 2(c)), the interference pattern once again vanishes. The screen now displays two bands, just as in the classical case! This is not what we expect. Both the slits are open, and we are not doing anything to close the superposition as in the Mach–Zehnder interferometer; thus we should expect interference to occur, and the fringes to appear on the photographic screen. It is as if observing the photon forces it to choose a single path, preventing it from interfering with itself and thus _destroying its quantum coherence_. Is quantum superposition so fragile?

Before moving on to the understanding of why measurements are so problematic for superposition, it is helpful to see how we keep account of these phenomena from a mathematical point of view. What must the equation of motion look like for a quantum system in order to account for such a peculiar phenomenon like superposition? Both the double-slit experiment and the Mach–Zehnder interferometer discussed above show a peculiar “wave-like” behaviour of the photon. It is from the wave theory that the terms “quantum interference” and “quantum coherence” are borrowed, and it is expected that the new equation of motion for quantum systems should have something in common with the equation that we use to describe waves. This was exactly the line of reasoning adopted by the Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger, who introduced the evolution equation governing a quantum system in 1926. This is known as the Schrödinger equation:[16]
(2) iℏd/dt|ψ⟩ = Ĥ|ψ⟩.

Formally, this is equivalent to Newton’s second law of motions for classical systems, but applies to quantum system instead.[17] A crucial feature of this equation is its linearity. While linearity is common to many physical theories, its role in quantum mechanics is fundamentally different. In classical physics, linear combinations of solutions describe alternative configurations of commuting physical quantities (_c-numbers_).[18] In quantum mechanics, by contrast, observables are represented by non-commuting operators (_q-numbers_) acting on a complex vector space of states. Linearity therefore applies to the space on which q-numbers act, rather than to definite configurations of physical quantities. As a consequence, if two quantum states are solutions of the Schrödinger equation, any linear combination represents a physically distinct state—irreducible to a classical mixture and capable of interference. In physical terms, this implies that a system can exist in a superposition of different states, each evolving consistently according to the same underlying law. Thus, the Schrödinger equation naturally accounts for the uncertainty principle: by allowing superpositions of states with different values of incompatible observables, it implies that such observables cannot, in general, possess simultaneously well-defined values.[19]
The Fragility of Quantumness: Fighting Quantum Decoherence

As we have seen, any measurement performed on a quantum system destroys its superposition, forcing the system into one of the possible alternatives with a certain probability. A measurement is nothing more than an _interaction_ between two physical systems: the quantum system under study and a measuring device. This interaction produces a definite outcome, recorded by the detector through a physical process that involves the detector alone. The disturbance of the quantum state, of the superposition, occurs precisely at the moment of interaction.

In this sense, _any_ interaction with the environment acts much like a measurement. Any external agent that couples to the quantum system inevitably perturbs its superposed state, forcing it to realise one of the possible alternatives that compose it. This phenomenon is known as _quantum decoherence_. Decoherence represents the greatest threat to the persistence of quantum properties in a system and is the principal reason why quantum effects are so difficult to observe beyond the microscopic scale. The larger and more complex the system is, the more numerous the interactions with its surroundings, and the more rapidly quantum coherence is lost. That’s why we do not see our beloved cat both dead and alive simultaneously, unlike Schrödinger’s one.

The fragility of quantum coherence raises a natural and profound question: if interaction with the environment inevitably destroys superposition, does there exist _a scale beyond which quantum mechanics ceases to apply?_

The importance of this question has been formally recognised by the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded to John Clarke, Michel H. Devoret, and John M. Martinis “for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit”.[20] Their work demonstrated that quantum effects, including _quantum tunnelling_ and discrete energy levels, can persist even in systems involving a large number of electrons, precisely where decoherence would be expected to suppress all non-classical behaviour.

The significance of this prize is not just related to the technological implications of the discovery—namely, the development of superconducting qubits, one of the most promising architectures for the development of quantum computers—but also to the foundational side of science. This result has pushed the limit at which quantum mechanics can safely be applied significantly further back. Investigating this limit is important for understanding the _universality_ of quantum theory in relation to the other pillar of modern physics, general relativity, which focuses on explaining reality at the scale where gravitational effects become relevant. Whether or not nonclassicality truly ends at some limit sheds light on one of the central challenges of theoretical physics, reconciling quantum mechanics and general relativity. This brings us to the role of macroscopic quantum mechanics.
Why Biology and Quantum Mechanics Were Thought to Be Forever Decoupled

The process of decoherence is thus not an accident or a technical inconvenience. Rather, it is the inevitable consequence of coupling a quantum system to the outside world. Given our above discussion, we should expect that there exist environments in which quantum coherence is so rapidly destroyed as to be effectively irrelevant. By all reasonable standards, _biological systems_ appear to fall squarely into this category.

Living matter operates at relatively high temperatures, in aqueous environments, and under constant interaction with complex and dynamic surroundings. Molecules collide, energy is exchanged, chemical reactions occur incessantly. Noise, disorder, and dissipation are not exceptional features of biology; they are its natural state. In such conditions, the number of possible interactions between a system of interest and its environment is enormous. Each interaction contributes to decoherence, rapidly erasing any phase information that might sustain quantum coherence.

From this perspective, it would seem almost inconceivable that delicate quantum features could survive for long enough to influence any biologically relevant process. Whatever quantum properties may exist at the level of individual atoms or molecules should be washed away long before they can play any functional role in the dynamics of life.

For this reason, quantum physics and biology were long regarded as belonging to fundamentally different conceptual domains. Quantum mechanics was seen as the theory of isolated, carefully controlled, microscopic systems—clean, cold, and weakly coupled to their environment. Biology, by contrast, was viewed as the realm of complexity, noise, irreversibility, and effective classicality.
Seen in this light, the very idea that quantum mechanics could be relevant to biological processes seemed at best implausible and at worst misguided.
This conclusion turns out to be premature.
When Does Quantum Mechanics Become Relevant to Biological Processes?
From the very birth of quantum theory, some of its pioneers sensed that the new physics might have implications that reached the scale of biological systems.[21]

In 1929, reflecting on the conceptual lessons quantum mechanics taught us about the “atomic and subatomic world” and aligning himself with organicist views claiming that the laws of physics and chemistry were sufficient to explain life’s mysteries, Niels Bohr remarked that:[22]

[T]he development of the atomic theory has [...] first of all given us a recognition of laws which cannot be included within the frame formed by our accustomed modes of perception; the lessons we have learned by the discovery of the quantum of action open up to us new prospects which may perhaps be of decisive importance, particularly in the discussion of the position of living organisms in our picture of the world.

The statement was deliberately cautious, but it hinted at a deeper possibility: that quantum mechanics could represent the “new physics” needed to understand the behaviour of living organisms and thus might force us to rethink the classical categories through which we describe Nature. This intuition was made more explicit in the early 1930s by Pascual Jordan, one of the founders of quantum mechanics, who posed a question that was deeply unsettling at the time: are the laws of quantum physics of essential importance for the processes of life? He even introduced the term _Quantenbiologie_, German for _Quantum Biology_, to describe this line of thought.[23] But without experimental support and burdened by speculative interpretations, the idea remained largely philosophical—a provocation rather than a research programme. A more concrete formulation appeared in 1944, when Erwin Schrödinger published _What is Life?_[24] Seeking to understand the extraordinary stability and fidelity of biological processes, specifically genetic inheritance, Schrödinger argued that the familiar statistical laws of thermodynamics—which he called “order from disorder”—were insufficient. Life, he suggested, must rely on a different principle, one capable of maintaining order at the level of small numbers of atoms. His famous image of the “aperiodic crystal”, consisting of groups of atoms, captured a key insight: biological function may depend on microscopic structures whose behaviour cannot be averaged away by thermal noise. In modern terms, Schrödinger was pointing towards a regime in which quantum dynamics, rather than being suppressed, could remain relevant precisely because a limited number of degrees of freedom are involved.

Despite these early insights, the idea that quantum mechanics might play a non-trivial role in biology gradually fell out of favour. Molecular biology flourished using the language of classical chemistry, while physics focused on isolated, controllable systems far removed from the complexity of living matter. For much of the twentieth century, the prevailing view was that any genuinely quantum features would be rapidly erased by decoherence in the “warm, wet, and noisy environment” of the cell. This was emphasised in the collection of essays, _What is Life: The Next Fifty Years_,[25] published after a conference marking the fiftieth anniversary since the Schrödinger’s lecture that inspired the original book, where quantum mechanics is largely absent as a possible explanatory framework for biological processes.

The situation began to change only towards the end of the twentieth century. Advances in experimental techniques, most notably ultrafast spectroscopy,[26] made it possible to probe molecular dynamics on timescales comparable to those of quantum coherence itself. At the same time, theoretical developments in the physics of open quantum systems provided a more nuanced understanding of decoherence, revealing that the interaction with the environment need not always be purely destructive.[27]

A small number of experiments began to challenge the longstanding assumption that coherence must vanish almost instantaneously in biological settings. In certain systems, quantum effects appeared to survive not only under warm and noisy conditions, but also on timescales relevant to biological function. This was a subtle but crucial shift. The question was no longer whether biology violates the principles of quantum mechanics—it does not—but whether, in specific contexts, living systems might operate in regimes where quantum features remain dynamically relevant.

What makes this shift particularly significant is that biological systems are not generic macroscopic systems. They possess a feature that radically distinguishes them from most physical systems studied in the laboratory: they are the product of _billions of years of evolution_. In living organisms, structure and dynamics are not accidental. They are the outcome of a long process of variation and selection, during which even small functional advantages can be amplified and stabilised over time. This introduces the additional actor of evolutionary theory into the picture, fundamentally altering the way we should think about the relevance of quantum effects in biology. If a quantum phenomenon were merely present but functionally irrelevant, it would be unlikely to persist. But if, under certain conditions, coherence, tunnelling, or other non-trivial quantum features could enhance the efficiency, robustness, or reliability of a biological process, then evolution would have had both the time and the incentive to exploit them. In this sense, the question is not whether biological systems are _allowed_ to display quantum behaviour according to the laws of physics, but whether natural selection may have shaped them to operate precisely in regimes where such behaviour becomes evolutionarily advantageous.
Photosynthesis: A Paradigmatic Example of Possible Non-Trivial Quantum Effects in Living Systems

Among biological processes suspected to have evolved in a way to exploit quantum effects is _photosynthesis_, the ultimate process that powers up life. This process of converting solar light into forms that are useful for the system’s survival is divided into two main stages:

_Light-harvesting stage_: a network of light-absorbing pigments, known as _chromophores_, absorbs solar light and funnels the resulting excitation towards a _reaction centre_. This network is called “light-harvesting antenna”.[28]

_Photochemical-to-chemical energy conversion stage_: in the reaction centre, the molecular excitations determined by the solar energy is converted into long-lived chemical energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH),[29] which subsequently fuel the capture and reduction of CO₂.[30],[31]

The second stage—photochemical-to-chemical energy conversion—is fairly inefficient, since not all incoming light is absorbed, and not all absorbed energy is converted into biomass.[32] However, the first stage is remarkably efficient: nearly every absorbed photon successfully contributes to charge separation at the reaction centre, initiating the downstream chemical reactions.

The suspicion that something beyond a purely classical mechanism might be at play in the light-harvesting stage did not arise from theoretical speculation alone, but from a slowly increasing number of mismatches between experimental observations and available models. Early descriptions of excitation energy transfer treated the process as an _incoherent hopping_ of energy between chromophores, an approach that successfully captured average transfer rates but implicitly assumed a rapid loss of phase information. In these models, no superposition was involved at any stage; the excitation is always _localised on a single chromophore_, following a _single path_ at any given time and migrating through the network by stochastic transitions between sites (see Fig. 3(a)). Different classical models correspond to different physical regimes, depending on the coupling strengths between chromophores and their interaction with the surrounding environment. At one extreme lies Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), applicable when chromophores are weakly coupled via Coulombic interactions and are largely separated. At the other extreme lies Redfield theory, which describes strongly coupled chromophores weakly interacting with their environment. Between these limits, a variety of intermediate models exist, designed to capture systems with moderate coupling and environmental interaction.

However, the advent of ultrafast spectroscopic techniques, capable of resolving dynamics on femtosecond timescales (10⁻¹⁵s), has revealed oscillatory features in the optical response of photosynthetic complexes that persist longer than expected in a warm and noisy biological environment. The optical response is the signal coming from the time evolution of the absorption and emission spectra of the tested system when excited with a sequence of extremely short laser pulses. Instead of decaying smoothly, the measured signal shows regular oscillations in time—essentially _beats_—with well-defined frequencies.[33],[34] These observations suggested that electronic excitations might remain partially _delocalised across several chromophores_ during their migration towards the reaction centre. In other words, superposition is playing a crucial role in efficiently guiding the excitation from the absorbing chromophores to the reaction centre. Within this emerging picture, the excitation does not explore the network sequentially, site by site. Rather, it can be present at multiple chromophores simultaneously, just as the photon passes through both the slits in the double-slit experiment of Fig. 2. The excitation explores multiple pathways in parallel, exactly as the photon was in both arms of the Mach–Zehnder interferometer in Fig. 1. This prompted a reinterpretation of light harvesting as an _open quantum dynamical process_, where coherence, environmental interactions, and dissipation coexist rather than exclude one another (see Fig. 3(b)). Within this framework, quantum coherence is not invoked as a fragile or exotic resource, but as a transient dynamical feature that may enhance transport robustness and efficiency under biological conditions. This provides a consistent explanation for how excitation energy is reliably funnelled to the reaction centre with near-unit quantum yield.

At the same time, it must be emphasised that this interpretation remains the subject of an active and unresolved debate.[35] Several authors have argued that the experimental signatures commonly associated with quantum coherence in light-harvesting complexes can, in principle, be reproduced by suitably refined classical or semiclassical models, without invoking any genuinely non-classical dynamics. In this view, the observed oscillations would emerge from correlated environmental fluctuations or from vibrational dynamics, rather than from long-lived quantum superpositions selected for by biological evolution.
Towards a New Methodology in Quantum Biology: Indirect Tests of Non-Classicality

It is precisely this ongoing debate that brings us back to the central methodological problem of quantum biology. Photosynthesis illustrates how difficult it is to distinguish between behaviour that merely _resembles_ quantum dynamics and behaviour that is _genuinely quantum_ in the sense of Definition 1. High efficiency, robustness to noise, and even oscillatory dynamics are not, by themselves, sufficient to establish non-classicality. Classical models, when enriched with environmental correlations or structured noise, can often reproduce similar phenomenology.

What is missing is a criterion capable of _ruling out all classical explanations_, independently of the microscopic details of the system. This is where the question of how to test non-classicality in biological systems becomes unavoidable.

Any convincing demonstration that photosynthetic energy transport exploits genuinely quantum features must therefore rely on tools that go beyond fitting models to experimental data. In particular, it must be based on criteria that are satisfied by all classical descriptions of the process—that is, by any description grounded in well-defined trajectories and mutually compatible observables. The key idea is to identify an effect that no such classical description can produce, but that becomes possible only if the system involved must be described by at least two incompatible observables. Observing such an effect would therefore rule out all classical explanations at once, independently of microscopic details, and establish the presence of a genuinely _quantum process_. An effect of this kind constitutes a definitive _witness of non-classicality_.

The difficulty lies in the very nature of biological systems. Unlike isolated quantum systems studied in the laboratory, biological structures cannot be prepared, controlled, or measured with arbitrary precision. Directly probing their microscopic degrees of freedom is often impossible, and any sufficiently invasive measurement would inevitably disrupt the process under investigation, inducing decoherence and destroying the very quantum process we are trying to uncover.
If quantum effects are present, they must therefore be identified _indirectly_.

To achieve this, we introduce a second system: a _quantum probe_ whose behaviour we can control and measure with high precision to _test_ the non-classical properties of the investigated process. The probe interacts with the biological system in such a way that any non-classical features of the biological process are imprinted onto the probe itself. In this sense, the quantum probe acts as a detective, investigating whether the process is quantum or not without disturbing it. The probe gathers clues that determine whether or not we must use two or more incompatible observables to describe the biological process under investigation. If the host biological system is genuinely quantum, it can mediate non-classical effects on the quantum probe that would otherwise be unattainable. If the probe exhibits such effects _under appropriate conditions_, then _all_ classical descriptions of the mediating process must be ruled out. We shall call this process a _witnessing task_ (see Fig. 4). Rather than attempting to directly measure the quantum states of the biological system itself—which would unavoidably disrupt its dynamics inducing decoherence—the witnessing task relies on measurements performed on a separate, wellcontrolled quantum probe. The focus is therefore not on the system’s internal state, but on what the biological process _can do_: whether it can mediate effects on the probe that no classical system could produce. The probe is measured only after the witnessing task has been completed.

The logic is very similar to that of Bell’s tests. In those, an inequality is derived under certain assumptions that makes the correlations between two subsystems compatible with a _classical_ description involving classical probability distributions, as in the case of the coin described above. However, if the correlations violate the inequality, then no classical description of them can be used to explain the phenomenon.[36] In the same way, if the witnessing task is _possible_ under the appropriate conditions, then there can be no classical description for it. This is exactly the kind of methodology we want for quantum biology: an indirect test capable of conclusively excluding any classical description of a biological process, even in the absence of the scientist’s detailed microscopic control. Such a methodology would indicate that Nature has evolved in a way to harness quantum effects for a biological advantage despite the “hot, wet and noisy” environment that would otherwise lead to decoherence.
Can we apply this logic to the light-harvesting stage of photosynthesis?
Temporal Witness of Non-Classicality and Its Applications to Biology

The idea is deceptively simple, and its power lies precisely in the fact that, when applied to light-harvesting in photosynthesis, it mirrors one of the most iconic experiments in the history of quantum physics, which we are now very familiar with: the double-slit experiment in Fig. 2. Recall that the only way to account for the emergence of an interference pattern on the photographic screen when both slits are open is to accept that the photon travels through both slits simultaneously, in a superposition of spatial paths thanks to its _quantum coherent_ evolution. As this is a genuinely quantum process that cannot be explained by any classical model, it is perfect to be our _witnessing task_.

Consider only the process of excitation transport in a photosynthetic complex and ignore the reaction centre. When a photon is absorbed by a light-harvesting antenna, it creates an excitation that propagates through a network of chromophores. As discussed earlier, there is compelling evidence that, at least transiently, this exciton may be delocalised over multiple chromophores rather than localised on a single site at any given time.

At first sight, this might seem very far removed from the simplicity of the double-slit experiment. Instead of a single photon travelling through empty space, we are dealing with a dense network of chromophores embedded in a protein scaffold, constantly interacting with a warm and fluctuating environment. And yet, at a conceptual level, the analogy can be made surprisingly precise.

When a photon is absorbed by the light-harvesting antenna, it disappears as an independent object and gives rise to an excitation of the molecular network: an _exciton_.[37] This exciton then propagates through the chromophores until it reaches the reaction centre. The crucial question concerns the nature of this propagation. Does the excitation move as a classical particle, hopping from one chromophore to the next along a single, well-defined path? Or can it exist in a superposition of different locations, simultaneously exploring multiple routes through the network?

If the latter is the case, then the exciton is doing exactly what the photon does in the double-slit experiment: it is not choosing one path but rather inhabiting several at once. The challenge, however, is that we cannot simply “look” at the exciton without destroying the very coherence we are trying to detect. Any direct attempt to determine where the excitation is localised would immediately collapse the superposition, just as placing a detector at one of the slits destroys the interference pattern. This is where the logic of an indirect test becomes essential.

Instead of probing the exciton directly, we allow it to act as a _mediator_ between two well-controlled quantum events. The photon that initially excites the antenna plays the role of a quantum probe. It is our quantum detective: Sherlock Photon. After being absorbed, it leaves behind an exciton whose subsequent evolution is governed by the internal dynamics of the biological complex. Later, through re-emission or through a controlled readout of the excitation, the photon’s degrees of freedom are retrieved. What we observe at the end is not the exciton itself, but the imprint it has left on the quantum probe: the non-classical effects it has mediated on the probe, the clues provided to the detective.

The key conceptual idea is to engineer the situation so that, during the exciton’s propagation, two distinct, spatially separated chromophores play the biological analogue of the two slits, as illustrated in Fig. 5. If the exciton were always localised on a single site, then selecting two chromophores would amount to nothing more than a classical mixture: the excitation would have passed through one site or the other, but never both. In that case, no interference could possibly arise. The effect we would see on a photographic screen is similar to the scenario in Fig. 2(b): a single stripe corresponding to the slit the photon went through, or in this case to the chromophore that the exciton was localised on. If, however, the exciton propagation is genuinely non-classical and delocalised across the network, then it would be on both selected chromophores simultaneously. When the photon is finally retrieved, the different paths taken by the exciton can interfere. This would give rise to an interference pattern in the statistics of the probe, exactly as in the double-slit experiment. Observing such interference would not be a statement about the photon alone, but about the nature of the process that mediated its evolution.
The Credibility of Sherlock Photon’s Clues: Conservation Laws

To be sure, this entire schema only works if it is combined with the appropriate assumptions. In this case, the assumptions must admit for a possibility that would invalidate the entire logic of the probe: the photon’s evolution must reflect faithfully that of the exciton. In other words, Sherlock Photon’s clues must be reliable. If this condition is not met, the quantum coherent evolution of the probe could be entirely unrelated to the biological dynamics we aim to investigate, rendering the witnessing task meaningless. In other words, we must exclude the possibility that the photon undergoes a coherent evolution that is independent of the biological system and its environment. To do so, we require a physical principle that _forces_ the probe, the biological system, and the environment to evolve consistently with one another.

This role is played by _conservation laws_. If the interaction between (i) the biological system, (ii) its surrounding environment, and (iii) the photon occurs under the conservation of a global physical quantity—for instance, the total energy—then any change in one part of the composite system must be accompanied by a corresponding change in the others. Under such conditions, the evolution of the photon cannot be decoupled from that of the exciton and its environment. Energy conservation is a particularly natural and welljustified assumption in this context. When it holds globally, any coherent evolution observed in the photon must be mediated by the biological system and its environment, elevating the quantum coherent evolution we record—Sherlock Photon’s clues—to the status of a witnessing task.
A Witnessing Theorem for Light-Harvesting in Photosynthesis
With these ingredients in place, we can summarise the core of this new proposal to witness quantum effects in biological processes as follows:[38]

Theorem 1. _If a photosynthetic system, together with its biological environment, can mediate the quantum coherent evolution of a photon under global energy-conserving dynamics, then the process of energy transfer in the lightharvesting phase of photosynthesis must engage a minimum of two incompatible degrees of freedom. In other words, the process must be non-classical._

The strength of this statement lies in its independence from detailed modelling. It does not specify _how_ quantum coherence is realised, nor which microscopic degrees of freedom are responsible for it. Instead, it establishes a _sufficient condition_: if the witnessing task is possible, then no classical description of the energy-transfer process can be valid.
This is precisely the kind of conclusion required to move the debate in quantum biology beyond phenomenology and model fitting.
Consequences and Outlook

The application of this new methodology, known as witnesses of nonclassicality,[39],[40] represents a potential turning point for quantum biology. By relying on information theoretic principles, such as the principle of locality and conservation laws (understood as constraints on how information and correlations can be mediated between physical systems independently of any dynamics assumption), this approach offers a way to answer the field’s central question in a decisive manner: _do quantum effects play a non-trivial role in biological processes?_ A successful application of this witness of non-classicality to biology would exclude _any_ possible classical description of the relevant process, since it would imply that, to account for the witnessing task, the biological system and its environment must have engaged at least two incompatible degrees of freedom. Such a result would constitute the second major application of non-classicality witnesses, following their use in the Bose–Marletto–Vedral effect, also known as gravitationally-induced entanglement, in quantum gravity.[41],[42]

The experiment proposal outlined here is within reach of current technology.[43] It relies on the interference fringes produced by an initially well-localised quantum detective: Sherlock Photon. If observed, these fringes would provide conclusive evidence that the biological system and its environment contributed incompatible observables to mediate the probe’s evolution. This would represent the first unambiguous demonstration that natural evolution has found a way to exploit quantum effects in functional biological processes, despite operating in conditions traditionally thought to be hostile to coherence.

Answering this long-standing question would open a number of relevant further questions that will shape the future not only of quantum biology, but also that of macroscopic quantum mechanics and quantum technologies. Specifically, what is the _precise_ quantum mechanism underlying the light-harvesting stage of photosynthesis? The witness of non-classicality in Theorem 1 does not tell us. It establishes that the process is certainly quantum, but it does not discriminate _between_ possible mechanisms. This implies that we could not distinguish where the incompatible observables needed for the photons’ quantum evolution come from: do they arise from the lightharvesting antenna as a whole, or from a single chromophore? What role does the environment play in this process? If it is helping the biological system to sustain quantum coherence for long enough to be relevant for biological processes, _how_ is it doing so?

These questions extend well beyond quantum biology and are essential for the broader field of macroscopic quantum mechanics. They directly inform the theory of open quantum systems, where understanding the role of environmental interactions is crucial. In particular, they address how such interactions can be shaped so that the environment does not merely induce decoherence, but can instead sustain quantum dynamics. If such interactions can be understood and engineered, they could inspire new applications that mimic biological processes and lay the groundwork for the creation of more efficient technologies in energy transport, absorption, and information processing. These bio-inspired quantum technologies could represent the future of industry, as they would benefit from the most knowledgeable and experienced teacher: Nature itself. If Nature has had billions of years to perfect its own mechanisms, why shouldn’t we learn from it to do the same?

Before tackling these broader challenges, however, the foundational question of quantum biology must be answered. The methodology based on witnesses of non-classicality provides a powerful and principled route towards this goal. Quantum biology, once regarded as speculative or even misguided, has matured into a field where precise theoretical tools and experimentally testable predictions can be formulated. With approaches such as the one presented here, it has never been closer to delivering a definitive answer.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic description of a Mach–Zehnder interferometer. A photon enters the optical device along the arm labelled “0” and reaches the first beam splitter (BS1). This beam splitter creates a superposition of the photon’s position, which will now travel along the two arms “0” and “1” simultaneously. The photon is then reflected by the mirrors (M) before reaching a second beam splitter (BS2), identical to the first. BS2 will close the superposition, allowing the two branches to interfere. The interference is detected by the detectors D0 and D1, placed along each of the two arms.

Figure 2: Schematic description of the double-slit experiment with photons. (a) Both the slits are open, and no observation is performed. The photons go through both of them simultaneously, in a superposition, generating the interference picture on the photographic screen. (b) One of the slits is now closed, and we do not observe the photon at any stage before the detection. The interference fringes on the photographic screen disappear, leaving room for a single stripe corresponding to the open slit. (c) Both the slits are open, but we measure which one each photon goes through. On the photographic screen we see two stripes, corresponding to the two open slits. Only (a) manifests quantum coherence.

Figure 3: A classical vs. quantum mechanism for the light-harvesting stage of photosynthesis. (a) Classical mechanisms do not allow for superpositions, so the exciton will “hop” from one site to the other, being localised on a single chromophore at each time. (b) With quantum mechanisms, superposition allows the exciton to be delocalised across multiple chromophores, exploring multiple paths simultaneously.

Figure 4: Schematic representation of a witnessing task in a biological setting. A controllable quantum probe interacts with an extended biological system, here represented as a network of sites. The joint evolution of probe, biological system, and environment is assumed to obey a global conservation law. The probe is measured only after the task has been completed. If the observed effect on the probe violates all classical constraints, the mediating biological process must be non-classical.

Figure 5: A schematic description of the experiment testing the witness of non-classicality in the light-harvesting stage of photosynthesis. A photon is initially absorbed by the chromophores it interacts with, being localised in a certain region of the antenna. The exciton it creates will propagate on the sample, following some mechanism. If such a mechanism involves quantum coherence, the exciton will be delocalised across multiple chromophores in the complex. After recombination, the emitted photon will generate an interference picture when spatially separated chromophores are selected by two slits.

chapters.title: 6 — Quantum Physics and General Relativity as Superinformation
paragraphs: Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

We review and extend the concept of superinformation as defined in constructor theory, arguing that physical systems in both quantum physics and general relativity can be seen as constituting superinformation media. Our analysis shows that the underlying information-theoretic structures of these two theories are closer than usually thought and can be described by the same set of counterfactuals. We then outline how this fact may pave the way to quantising gravity.
Introduction

It is often said that quantising gravity is difficult because the basic principles of quantum physics and general relativity are fundamentally different and therefore irreconcilable. Various differences are listed to illustrate such incompatibilities between the two most fundamental theories we have at present. For instance, we are told that the superposition principle and the equivalence principle contradict one another; or that the principle of general relativistic invariance (diffeomorphism invariance) is incompatible with the existence of local observables, which are fundamental in quantum field theory.[1] Or, the converse, namely that general relativity is a local theory and that quantum physics is non-local. And so on. While we do not subscribe to any of these arguments, rather than falsifying them one by one (which we have done elsewhere [1]), here we focus on the similarities.

It is true that quantum theory’s pillar, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, prescribes that physical variables of a quantum system cannot be all sharp at any given time; in particular, it is impossible to specify with an arbitrarily high accuracy all the relevant variables (meaning that they cannot be measured simultaneously to an arbitrary accuracy, as we will detail below). In contrast, in both special and general relativity, physical variables at a point in spacetime can be all sharp and are all jointly measurable with arbitrarily high accuracy. In other words, the information-theoretic structure of relativity is classical. This, of course, is not an obstacle to quantising gravity; rather it provides a reason for doing so.

In this paper, we shall explore the fact that quantum physics and general relativity are, surprisingly, in curious agreement. This becomes manifest when considering their information-theoretic structure from a broader, counterfactual perspective. Informally, the idea is this. In quantum physics, we can define as _classical_ any commuting subset of the full set of allowed quantum observables. For instance, a single qubit confined to measurements of observables that all commute with the z component of the spin (arbitrarily chosen as the classical direction in this case) is classical in this sense. This is because all the observables in that set can be measured jointly to arbitrarily high accuracy. Hence, any qubit contains infinitely many ways of instantiating a classical bit of information, each corresponding to one possible orientation of the spin axis. Once a classical context is chosen, quantumness (or non-classicality) is then described as a deviation from that classical context. In fact, each spin direction provides a basis for a different classical context. Quantum effects can then be seen as “connections” between these classical contexts, represented by unitary transformations. (Unitary transformations are linear, one-to-one transformations that preserve the inner product of vectors.)

In general relativity, on the other hand, spacetime is locally flat (Minkowski), while it may not be flat overall. One can consider flat spacetime at any given spacetime point as the general relativistic analogue of a classical context. Non-classicality in this case is the deviation from flat spacetime, quantified by curvature. Gravity, expressed as non-trivial (curved) spacetime geometry, is then seen as connecting all the locally flat manifolds. In other words, gravity in general relativity plays the role of non-commutativity between different classical contexts in quantum physics. Spacetime then corresponds to what in unitary quantum theory is called the multiverse. In this article we shall discuss how this non-classicality can be interpreted in constructor-information-theoretic terms, as the impossibility of performing certain measurement tasks.

Closely related ideas have been proposed in the past from time to time—see e.g., Isham’s topos theory [2]. However, in those other approaches, the ontology of quantum theory is probabilistic and centred on outcomes of measurements; it is broadly informed by the Copenhagen interpretation. Here, instead, we take unitary quantum theory to be the foundation: our ontology is therefore made of q-numbers, representing the quantum observables of a quantum system. This choice is well-known to have many advantages in both quantum field theory and non-relativistic quantum theory, particularly because it allows one to explicitly satisfy locality as intended by Einstein [3], in the Heisenberg picture. We shall also use the methodology of the constructor theory of information, which is a key tool to describe quantum and classical systems in a unifying framework. Remarkably, it does not use any particular formalisms or dynamics, but only constraints about possible/impossible tasks.

The fact that locally flat Minkowski spacetimes are, in a welldefined sense to be explored here, analogous to the classical domains in quantum physics, has led to two different approaches to quantising gravity. One is via logic, in which case one looks for the “curved” generalisation of Boolean logic that underpins classical physics. Topos theory was developed exactly for this purpose. In this type of logic, Boolean logic holds “locally”, while globally the logic is more general (i.e., non-binary). The origins of this approach are in von Neumann’s quantum logic [[2], [4], [5]].

Another approach is via geometry: one can take the Riemannian structure of general relativity and imprint it on quantum physics. Such approaches to geometrise quantum physics (by defining quantum metrics, geodesics, and parallel transport) were popular in the sixties, but, much like quantum logic itself, they ultimately failed to deliver a unification of quantum physics and general relativity [[6], [7]].

We therefore believe that a different approach is necessary. We shall argue that the concept of information proves fruitful in describing the non-classicality of quantum physics and, at the same time, the non-flatness of spacetime in the presence of gravity. The rest of the paper is organised as follows: we first review the constructor theory of information that is at the core of the “isomorphism” between quantum physics and general relativity. Then we apply it to quantum physics, followed by general relativity, to demonstrate the isomorphism. Finally, we discuss the implications of our work for quantum gravity programmes.
Superinformation

First, we review superinformation as defined in constructor theory, which allows one to express non-classicality in a way that avoids assuming all the formal baggage of quantum theory [[9]–[11]]. This shift is key here, as the _dynamical_ features of quantum theory (such as Hilbert spaces, state vectors, and the like) may not survive in quantum gravity, while the _information-theoretic_ phenomena displayed by quantum systems are expected to be relevant (that is, those that distinguish quantum information and computation from their classical counterparts). So we need to be able to describe quantumness/nonclassicality without committing to the whole of quantum theory’s formalism. The constructor theory of information, particularly with the idea of superinformation theories, allows one to do that in an elegant and concise manner by appealing to counterfactuals. Moreover, we think that the constructor theory of information, by imposing conditions on what physical systems can contain possibly information, provides the foundations for logic itself; the latter usually assumes distinguishability of states to be primitive, while here we consider a more general setting where distinguishability is a derivative concept. The details of the construction are as follows.

An information medium is a physical system with a set of distinct attributes (sets of states) that 1) can be permuted in all possible ways, and 2) can be faithfully copied [9] (see also the appendix for a summary of the more formal details). Note that in the original definitions, these requirements are intended to hold locally in spacetime (i.e., at a given spacetime point). Here we speculate on a possible extension to the case where a non-trivial spacetime geometry plays a role, which, as we shall discuss, provides a novel angle on the task of quantising gravity. Such permutable and copiable attributes constitute an information variable. Indeed, because of the copiability requirement, the attributes in an information variable have to be distinguishable in the standard sense [9]— e.g., in quantum theory, they correspond to sets of mutually orthogonal subspaces. In classical physics (at least, a discretised version of it), it is clear that the set of all states of a physical system qualify as an information variable, because all classical states can in principle be perfectly distinguished. Even if we do not know the position and momentum of a particle, we can think of a dynamical scenario in which both are faithfully imprinted on another particle up to any arbitrarily high given accuracy. The reversible classical computation, such as its implementation in the Toffoli billiard ball computer, is a consequence of the fact that all classical states are copiable and therefore constitute an information variable.

However, Nature allows us to go beyond this basic concept of classical information. While the position eigenstates are an information variable in quantum mechanics and, separately, the momentum eigenstates constitute another information variable, taken together they no longer qualify as an information variable. The reason is that positions and momenta can be copied separately, but their set-union cannot be: the Heisenberg uncertainty principle prevents us from doing so.

Formally, a superinformation medium is an information medium with the property that the union of two or more of its information variables is not an information variable. A quantum system (e.g., a qubit) constitutes a superinformation medium because states in quantum mechanics cannot in general be copied (see the no-cloning theorem [12]). It is therefore not a surprise that quantum systems are superinformation media (it was proven in [[9]–[11]]). What is surprising is that spacetime geometry as described by general relativity also conforms to the notion of superinformation (but for a different reason from quantum systems). We shall now explain why.
Quantum Superpositions as Superinformation

Different eigenstates of every quantum observable are orthogonal to each other and therefore can be used as information variables. In fact, the classical limit of quantum physics corresponds exactly to the most general set of commuting observables so that, taken together, they still qualify as an information variable [13]. This is because, ultimately, all commuting observables share the same basis of distinguishable states that can be faithfully copied.

One can always choose any of the commuting observables for an experimental setup. Upon measuring that observable, one sees a sharp outcome (with some probability) relative to that measurement. In this case, relative to that outcome, complementary observables become unsharp.

Sets of eigenstates of any two observables that do not commute with each other are not an information variable, because they cannot be jointly faithfully copied/measured. That is because an eigenstate of a given observable is a superposition of eigenstates of a different, non-commuting observable. When one is sharp, the other cannot be sharp. This is a formal way of defining a superposition to be a nonclassical feature of quantum physics. It is possible to show that all key features of quantum theory follow from the simple requirement constraining superinformation media: the union of two information variables is not an information variable itself [9]. Furthermore, while one observer may choose one set of commuting observables as defining their information variable locally to them, another observer may choose a different set of commuting observables as their local information variable. It is the correlations between the two information variables that could reveal the existence of superinformation at the level of two information variables taken together. In this case, the manifestation of superinformation is through quantum entanglement.
Curvature as Superinformation

We shall now discuss how superinformation has a non-trivial instantiation in spacetime geometry and gravity. First, we need to identify what counts as an information variable—sets of states that can be copied in an ordinary way, which defines classicality. Then, we identify superinformation as a deviation from classicality (defined via information variables). In general relativity, spacetime is locally Minkowski/flat [14]. In other words, spacetime geometry can be point-wise approximated by a flat manifold. Hence there is always a coordinate system in which we can locally gauge away gravity. Another way to state this fact is that a coordinate system falling in gravity is inertial as far as Einstein’s theory is concerned. This is one possible way to express the equivalence principle. We shall see that the equivalence principle is the key counterfactual principle that, in general relativity, plays the role of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. It is the very reason for why something akin to superinformation arises in general relativity. Let us now elaborate on this idea, which is the core of this paper.

First, we need to define classicality in terms of copiable sets of states, where copiable must be defined here in a suitable manner. We suggest that the information variables here are defined with respect to inertial systems as copiable sets of states, where the relevant copying is defined as follows: copying a state of a system in such a coordinate system consists of preparing another system in the same state of motion in that coordinate system. This definition of copiability is local (point-like) in spacetime. In fact, the trajectories of all particles that are falling under gravity in the vicinity of each other are “copies” of one another. Likewise for copiable trajectories at another spacetime point. This defines classicality in the gravitational scenario.

What is, then, superinformation? We need to identify states that cannot be copied in the above sense. Remarkably, this can be done naturally: for the union of all such trajectories no longer constitutes an information variable, because they cannot be jointly copied in the sense defined above. This is because gravity (non-trivial spacetime geometry) does not allow one to put together different Minkowski/flat coordinate systems without “twisting” them. This necessary twist, which originates with the curvature of spacetime geometry, is the origin of what we propose to call “gravitational superinformation”. This impossibility of copying, in turn, is implied by the equivalence principle, which says that it is impossible to tell gravity from acceleration with only local measurements. If you were able to copy, in the sense defined above, the trajectories at different spacetime points, then you would violate the impossibility requirement at the foundation of the equivalence principle.

In other words, one needs a parallel-transport transformation[2] between the two local frames in order to make the copying of the trajectories possible. In order to define _that_ transformation, you need the details of the spacetime geometry. Likewise, in quantum theory, unitary rotations relate the two classical contexts to one another and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle in quantum theory forbids copying. In that sense, parallel transport in general relativity corresponds to unitarity in quantum physics; the equivalence principle to Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle.
Towards an Information-Theoretic Unification of Quantum Physics and General Relativity

Given that the key quantum feature, that of superposition, and the key gravitational feature, that of curvature, can both be seen as instances of superinformation, the question arises as to whether this fact makes it easier to unify the two theories. A summary of our comparison between quantum theory and relativity is given in the table below.
Information-Theoretic Notions Quantum Theory General Relativity
Counterfactual constraints Heisenberg Uncertainty Equivalence Principle
Structure-preserving evolution Unitary Transformation Parallel Transport
Superinformation non-classicality Non-commutativity Non-zero Curvature
Classical limit Commuting Variables Flat Spacetime

Superinformation constitutes the excess information that exists beyond the “ordinary” copiable, classical information. Could the quantum superinformation be the same as the gravitational superinformation? The non-commutativity that gives us the quantum superinformation, SI_Q, could be thought of as the excess quantum information power over its classical equivalent; for gravity, there would be a corresponding SI_G. It would be an interesting challenge (which we leave for future studies) to formally relate these two quantities. We strongly suspect that solving this problem might be at the heart of quantising gravity. Note that we are not here suggesting that quantum effects in gravity are emergent (as in [15]), or that one can dispense with quantising gravity. In fact, we think that digging deeper into this analogy will indicate a fruitful path for quantising gravity, based on the information-theoretic structure of quantum theory and relativity.

The analogy is compelling, but it leaves open questions. In quantum theory, unitaries can permute all elements of the union of two non-compatible/complementary information variables. This is what allows one to perform quantum computations. It is also what causes (together with the no-cloning theorem) the existence of entanglement, expressed most dramatically in the existence of a global information variable (like the Bell basis) that is not an information variable locally. Does this property also exist in the case of gravity? To have a full analogy, one would have to find objects equivalent to the Bell states in the case of gravity, where one has a globally sharp observable arising jointly while having what one may call “gravitational locally inaccessible information”. This is an open question, and we think that answering it may give us further clues as to how to successfully quantise gravity.

So while it is still possible to quantify the “non-classicality” of gravity using the same measures as for non-classicality in quantum information, the two ways of departing from classicality still mean something different in each domain. Would the quantisation of gravity provide the bridge? Quantum gravity pioneer Bryce De Witt pointed out that key to unlocking the quantisation of gravity is the understanding of the information-theoretic foundations of both quantum theory and relativity and identifying observables in both theories [16]. This problem has not been solved to this day. We think the approach we outlined, based on constructor theory, opens up the possibility of properly understanding observables in gravity in the information-theoretic, counterfactual sense. We hope that this move shall open a much-needed novel perspective on the problem of quantising gravity.
Appendix

In this appendix we summarise several fundamental formal elements of constructor theory, which are presented in detail in [[9]–[11]]. An _attribute_ x is defined as a set of states sharing a common property _x_. For instance, in quantum theory, the collection of all qubit states for which a given projector Π is sharp with eigenvalue 1 constitutes an attribute.

A _variable_ is a collection of mutually disjoint attributes. Let a be an attribute of a substrate S₁ and b an attribute of a substrate S₂. The composite attribute (a, b) of the combined substrate S₁ ⊕ S₂ is defined as the set of all states in which S₁ possesses attribute a and S₂ possesses attribute b. By Einstein’s locality principle, if a transformation acts exclusively on S₁, then only attribute a can change, while b remains invariant [9].
A _task_ is defined as a finite collection of ordered pairs of input and output attributes.

A _constructor_ for a task T is a system that, whenever the substrate is prepared in one of the input attributes of T, transforms it into a state belonging to the corresponding output attribute, while _preserving the ability to perform the same transformation repeatedly_. A task is termed impossible _if_ the laws of physics impose a fundamental restriction preventing its accurate execution by any constructor; otherwise, the task is said to be _possible_. Constructor theory concerns itself exclusively with the possibility or impossibility of tasks, independently of the particular physical realisation, and is therefore scale- and dynamics-independent. Tasks obey an algebraic structure [10]. Two tasks T₁ and T₂ may be composed either serially—when the output attributes of T₁ coincide with the input attributes of T₂—or in parallel, according to the usual meanings of these operations [9]. Serial composition is denoted by T₁T₂, while parallel composition is written as T₁ ⊗ T₂. The transpose of a task T, denoted T^∼, is obtained by reversing each input–output pair. It follows immediately that (T^∼)^∼ = T and (T₁ ⊗ T₂)^∼ = T₁^(∼) ⊗ T₂^(∼). A central principle of constructor theory, known as the _composition law_, asserts that the composition of two possible tasks is itself possible.
A Quantum-Theory Model for Possible Tasks

We now describe a quantum model of a constructor, following [10]. Consider a composite quantum system consisting of subsystems C and S, with total Hilbert space H = H_C ⊗ H_S. Let U be a fixed unitary operator governing their interaction. For a projector X, we denote by Σ(X) its +1 eigenspace. For any operator B, define B^((C)) = B ⊗ I and B^((S)) = I ⊗ B. Let x = Σ(X^((S))) and y = Σ(Y^((S))) be two attributes of S, where X and Y are orthogonal projectors.
Each attribute corresponds to the set of states of S in which the associated projector is sharp with value 1 . Define the task T = x→ y. We introduce the following set of states of C :

This set comprises those states of C such that, when C is prepared in one of them and interacts with S in any state |x⟩ ∈ Σ(X^((S))), the resulting evolution maps S into a state with attribute y. In general, the final state may be entangled, and the system C may lose its ability to perform the transformation repeatedly. It is straightforward to show that V_T is a vector space. For C to function as a constructor for the task A_T, the following conditions must be satisfied:
V_T is non-empty;
There exists a subspace W_T ⊆ V_T such that

The second condition guarantees that states in W_T preserve their ability to implement the task T indefinitely. Let Π_(W_T) denote the orthogonal projector onto the smallest subspace W_T ⊆ H_C satisfying this requirement. If these conditions are met, one can define the nonempty set

which is itself a vector space. States in this subspace either lie in W_T or are mapped into it after a single application of U. The projector Π_(C_T) onto V_(C_T) thus acts as the _projector for being a constructor_ for the task A_T. Therefore, the possibility of a task T within quantum theory implies the existence of a subspace V_(C_T) satisfying the conditions above.
Constructor Theory of Information
We conclude by summarising key results from the constructor theory of information, following [9, 11]. The cloning task for a variable X is defined as

where ⋃ denotes set union and x₀ is a fixed attribute. The variable X is said to be _copiable_ if the task C(X) is possible for some choice of x₀. In quantum theory, this is the case if and only if all elements of X are mutually orthogonal; otherwise, the task is impossible. As an example, if _X_ = {0, 1} is a Boolean variable and x₀ = 0, the task C(X) can be implemented using a controlled-NOT gate. This construction generalises the standard quantum cloning task. An information medium is a substrate for which both the cloning task C(X) and the permutation task

are possible for all permutations Π of the labels of the attributes in X, for some attribute x₀ ∈ X. In quantum theory, any set of orthogonal states lacking additional symmetries or superselection rules constitutes an information variable. The task C(X) corresponds to the copying, or cloning, of the attribute of the first substrate onto a second target substrate, while Π(X) represents a logically reversible computation. For example, a qubit equipped with any pair of orthogonal states, _X_ = {0, 1}, functions as an information medium. Finally, as discussed in the main text, a variable Y is said to be _distinguishable_ if the task
is possible, where the variable q_y has the same cardinality as Y and is itself an information variable.
